name: Ad Hominem
definition: Attacking the person making an argument instead of addressing the argument itself.
example: "You can't trust his opinion on the economy, he dropped out of college."
fix: Respond to the substance of the claim, not the character or background of the person making it.

name: Straw Man
definition: Misrepresenting an opponent's argument in a weaker or more extreme form, then attacking that instead.
example: "She wants better school funding? So she just wants to throw unlimited money at the problem."
fix: Restate the opponent's actual position accurately before responding to it.

name: Appeal to Authority
definition: Claiming something is true mainly because an authority figure or expert says so, without other supporting evidence.
example: "A famous actor says this diet works, so it must be effective."
fix: Cite the actual evidence or reasoning the authority relies on, not just their title or fame.

name: False Dilemma
definition: Presenting only two options when more possibilities actually exist.
example: "Either we ban the product completely, or we do nothing at all."
fix: Acknowledge the middle-ground or alternative options between the two extremes.

name: Slippery Slope
definition: Arguing that a small first step will inevitably lead to a chain of increasingly extreme, often unlikely, consequences.
example: "If we allow this one exception, soon there will be no rules left at all."
fix: Show the actual causal mechanism connecting each step, or acknowledge the chain isn't guaranteed.

name: Circular Reasoning
definition: An argument where the conclusion is just a restatement of the premise, so it proves nothing new.
example: "This law is just, because it's the law."
fix: Provide independent evidence for the premise that doesn't depend on the conclusion already being true.

name: Hasty Generalization
definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from a small or unrepresentative sample.
example: "I met two rude tourists from that country, so people from there are rude."
fix: Reference a larger, more representative body of evidence before generalizing.

name: Red Herring
definition: Introducing an unrelated topic to divert attention away from the original argument.
example: "Why worry about the budget deficit when crime rates are also a problem?"
fix: Stay on the original claim and address it directly before raising new topics.

name: Bandwagon
definition: Arguing a claim is true or good because many people believe or do it.
example: "Everyone is investing in this, so it must be a good idea."
fix: Provide evidence for the claim itself rather than pointing to its popularity.

name: Appeal to Emotion
definition: Using emotional appeals in place of logical reasoning to persuade.
example: "Think about the poor families who will suffer if this bill fails!"
fix: Pair the emotional point with concrete evidence or reasoning that supports the claim.

name: Tu Quoque
definition: Dismissing an argument by pointing out the arguer's own hypocrisy, rather than addressing the argument.
example: "You say I should recycle more, but you drove here today."
fix: Address whether the claim is true regardless of the arguer's own consistency.

name: Genetic Fallacy
definition: Judging an idea as true or false based on its origin rather than its current merits.
example: "That theory came from a controversial scientist, so it can't be right."
fix: Evaluate the claim on its current evidence, independent of where it originated.

name: No True Scotsman
definition: Redefining a group to exclude counterexamples after a generalization about that group is challenged.
example: "No real environmentalist would ever fly on a plane."
fix: Keep the definition of the group fixed instead of adjusting it to dodge counterexamples.

name: Begging the Question
definition: Assuming the truth of the conclusion within the premise itself.
example: "Free speech is important because people should be free to say what they want."
fix: Support the premise with a reason that doesn't already assume the conclusion.

name: Post Hoc
definition: Assuming that because one event followed another, the first must have caused the second.
example: "Crime dropped after the new mayor took office, so the mayor caused the drop."
fix: Rule out other possible causes or coincidences before claiming causation.

name: Ad Populum
definition: Appealing to widespread popular opinion as if it were proof of truth.
example: "Most citizens support this policy, so it must be the right choice."
fix: Separate what is popular from what is actually supported by evidence.

name: Appeal to Nature
definition: Claiming something is good or correct because it is 'natural', or bad because it is 'unnatural'.
example: "This remedy is natural, so it has to be safer than the manufactured medicine."
fix: Evaluate safety and effectiveness with evidence, not with how 'natural' something sounds.

name: Anecdotal Fallacy
definition: Using a single personal story or isolated example in place of solid evidence.
example: "My grandfather smoked his whole life and lived to 90, so smoking isn't that dangerous."
fix: Bring in broader data or studies rather than relying on one story.

name: Middle Ground
definition: Assuming that the truth must lie exactly between two opposing positions.
example: "One side says the treatment works, the other says it doesn't, so it must work half the time."
fix: Judge each position on its own evidence rather than assuming a compromise is correct.

name: Burden of Proof
definition: Shifting the responsibility of proof onto the other party instead of supporting one's own claim.
example: "You can't prove this policy won't work, so we should assume it will."
fix: Provide positive evidence for your own claim rather than demanding the other side disprove it.

name: Ad Ignorantiam
definition: Arguing a claim is true because it has not been proven false, or vice versa.
example: "No one has proven this isn't dangerous, so we should assume it is."
fix: Base the claim on positive evidence rather than an absence of disproof.

name: Appeal to Pity
definition: Attempting to win an argument by evoking sympathy rather than presenting evidence.
example: "You have to agree with me, I've worked so hard on this and it means everything to me."
fix: Support the claim with facts, and keep sympathy separate from the argument's merit.

name: Appeal to Fear
definition: Using fear or intimidation instead of evidence to push a conclusion.
example: "If we don't pass this law immediately, disaster is guaranteed."
fix: Provide evidence for the likelihood of the feared outcome rather than just invoking fear.

name: Guilt by Association
definition: Discrediting an idea by linking it to a disliked person or group, rather than addressing it directly.
example: "That policy sounds a lot like something an extremist group once proposed, so it must be bad."
fix: Assess the idea on its own merits, independent of who else may have suggested it.

name: Cherry Picking
definition: Selecting only the data or examples that support a conclusion while ignoring evidence that contradicts it.
example: "This one study supports my view, so I'll ignore the ten others that don't."
fix: Address the full body of evidence, including data that complicates or contradicts the claim.
